solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Stand out as model or poet

definitions.meaning: what makes an artist's model stand out: posing well, holding still
an English poet of the early twentieth century, sister of Osbert and Sacheverell

explanation.surface: A talent scout wonders whether a striking newcomer should become a model or a poet.
explanation.walkthrough: The first definition is a phrase, not a word: a model who can SIT WELL stands out. Edith Sitwell (1887-1964) was an English poet.
explanation.definitionFit: A phrase definition split into two words, plus a surname: sitting well is a model's whole job, and Edith Sitwell was a poet.

indicators.note: in a down clue the letter sits under the hero, holding it up

parts.note: a hero is an American long sandwich, also called a sub

explanation.surface: A hospital patient's letter of thanks props up the reputation of a heroic doctor.
explanation.walkthrough: Hero here is the sandwich, not a brave person; in American English a hero, sub and hoagie are the same long roll.
explanation.definitionFit: A loose synonym: a patient person puts up with things without protest, which shades into meekly yielding.

clue.text: Cleopatra was such a classic film

definitions.text: Cleopatra was such a classic film

parts.note: not the 1963 epic: read it as a statement about the woman, what kind of ruler she was and on which continent
the answer is also the title of a 1951 film with Bogart and Hepburn

explanation.surface: A film critic reflects that Cleopatra has always made for a classic movie.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface points at the film Cleopatra, but the clue means that Cleopatra herself, ruler of Egypt, was an African queen; The African Queen (1951) starred Bogart and Hepburn.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by example with a double reading: Egypt is in Africa, so its queen fits the phrase, which is also a famous film title.

indicators.note: loses its head, the first letter

explanation.surface: A grim report from a battlefield: an army was defeated, its leader beheaded, and the rest finished off.
explanation.walkthrough: The three words read as one grim list, but only the last is the definition; the first two are the wordplay.
explanation.definitionFit: An idiom for finishing food: to polish off a plate is to eat all of it.

parts.note: to last is to stay, endure

explanation.surface: A soldier is told to stay put after being ordered to retire.
explanation.walkthrough: The Last Post is the bugle call that sends British soldiers to their quarters for the night, so it is literally an order to retire.
explanation.definitionFit: A military sense: the bugle call is the signal for soldiers to retire, meaning go to bed.

clue.text: Made invalid call up, in a way

indicators.note: the first piece sits inside the second

parts.note: to evoke is to call up a memory

explanation.surface: An official cancelled a call-up that was made in a roundabout way.
explanation.walkthrough: Invalid sounds like a sick person, but it is the adjective: made invalid means cancelled.
explanation.definitionFit: A legal synonym: a revoked licence or order has been cancelled, so no longer valid.

clue.text: I will open shop in allotment

indicators.note: the I goes into the middle of the phrase, splitting it

parts.note: to shop someone is to rat on them

explanation.surface: Someone plans to open a little shop on their allotment.
explanation.walkthrough: Shop is the verb meaning to inform on someone. An allotment in Britain is also a rented vegetable plot, which the surface uses.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: a fixed share allotted to each person.

indicators.note: the pieces are fed into the word for pure

explanation.surface: A soldier who stays chaste is at least well fed.
explanation.walkthrough: Vestal comes from the Vestal Virgins of Rome. The 's on soldier means 'is', joining the pieces to fed.
explanation.definitionFit: A biological sense: a structure left over, still remaining from an earlier stage of evolution.

definitions.meaning: an idiom telling someone not to lose their temper
the same words taken literally: stay covered up; the question mark flags the jokey sense

explanation.surface: Advice for a hot day at the beach: stay cool and keep covered.
explanation.walkthrough: Stay cool sounds like advice about heat, but it is the idiom for keeping calm; only the second half is about the sun.
explanation.definitionFit: An idiom read two ways: calm down, and literally stay covered in the sun.

definitions.meaning: slang for a fist, as in 'put 'em up'
the highest rank of British nobility

explanation.surface: A boxer needs to win a title.
explanation.walkthrough: Boxing title reads as a championship belt, but it splits: a fist is needed for boxing, and the same word is a noble title. 'Put up your dukes' means raise your fists.
explanation.definitionFit: Two senses: slang for a fist, which a boxer can't do without, and a peer's title.

parts.note: lest = in case, as in lest we forget

explanation.surface: A holy book is kept in a protective case.
explanation.walkthrough: Holy book looks like one phrase for the Bible; in fact holy is the definition and book gives just B.
explanation.definitionFit: A poetic spelling of blessed, which means holy or sacred.

definitions.meaning: a phrase softening a figure of speech, 'as it were'
stitch is SEW, and a cryptic setter would say SEW sounds like SO

explanation.surface: A crossword solver explains how a setter might hint at the word stitch.
explanation.walkthrough: Split the answer: stitch means sew, and sew pronounced is 'so', so stitch is SO, to speak, which is how a cryptic clue would render it.
explanation.definitionFit: A stock phrase meaning 'as it were', and a literal reading: SO is stitch when spoken.

clue.text: Tiny star is cool, part of dying out

indicators.note: the letters are put out of order

parts.note: anagram of PART OF DYING, 11 letters

explanation.surface: An astronomer notes that a small star is cooling as part of dying out.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface is astronomy (small stars do cool as they die), but the star is a gifted child. Dying out reads as one phrase; out is the anagram indicator.
explanation.definitionFit: A playful definition: tiny means very young, and star means a brilliant performer.

clue.text: Publicity piece on new Conservative bill

parts.note: a promo is a publicity piece

explanation.surface: A publicity campaign is launched for a new Conservative bill in Parliament.
explanation.walkthrough: Bill looks like a law, but it is the narrow headland found in place names such as Portland Bill.
explanation.definitionFit: A regional geographic sense: a bill is a narrow headland, as in Portland Bill on the English coast.

clue.text: Please check out this item of luggage

parts.note: to case a place is to check it out, as a burglar does

explanation.surface: An airport notice asks passengers to check their bags out.
explanation.walkthrough: Please looks like a polite request, but it is the verb, as in 'suit yourself'.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain definition by category: the commonest kind of bag for travelling.

indicators.note: letters that are running about are rearranged

explanation.surface: A fell runner races over the hills around ancient sites.
explanation.walkthrough: Fell running is a British sport of racing over hills (a fell is a hill); here fell is the past tense of fall.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym in the past tense: to fall down in a heap.

indicators.note: the sweet goes without the letters ICE

parts.note: liquorice is a black chewy sweet

explanation.surface: A drinker asks for fruit juice with no ice.
explanation.walkthrough: Sweet juice reads as one thing, but sweet is the candy liquorice (licorice in American spelling).
explanation.definitionFit: A cooking sense: the liquid left from boiling or preserving, or pressed from fruit.

indicators.note: in a down clue the word is turned over, reading upwards

parts.note: to deal in goods is to SELL them; turned over

explanation.surface: A news report on an arms deal with the Contras, the Nicaraguan rebels, run through the West Indies.
explanation.walkthrough: WI is the standard abbreviation for the West Indies; the Antilles are its main island chain.
explanation.definitionFit: A proper name: the Greater and Lesser island chains make up most of the West Indies.

clue.text: Sound made by sailor entering base

indicators.note: the sailor goes into the word for base

explanation.surface: A noise is heard as a sailor walks into a naval base.
explanation.walkthrough: Sound here is the adjective, as in a sound plan, not a noise.
explanation.definitionFit: The adjective sense: a sound plan is workable, capable of succeeding.

clue.text: Filling lunch has replaced meals in America

indicators.note: the letters are placed again in a new order
the filling of a word is its middle

explanation.surface: A food writer notes that in America a filling lunch has taken the place of proper meals.
explanation.walkthrough: Filling lunch reads as a hearty lunch, but filling is the middle of LUNCH. Uncle Sam is the cartoon personification of the United States.
explanation.definitionFit: A personification: the bearded figure in the stars-and-stripes hat stands for the United States.

indicators.note: a word that is turned faces the other way, so its letters read backwards

parts.note: sex is Latin for six, VI in Roman numerals

explanation.surface: A cheeky line about someone finding what they see arousing.
explanation.walkthrough: Sex is not about the act at all: it is the Latin for six, which gives VI.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: the faculty of sight.

definitions.meaning: a rider is a clause added to a statement or contract that limits it
an ability or credential that fits you for a job

explanation.surface: A jockey's riding ability is on show.
explanation.walkthrough: Rider suggests a jockey, but it is the added clause in a contract or statement that limits it.
explanation.definitionFit: Two senses: a limiting condition on a statement, and an accomplishment that makes you fit for a role.

parts.note: not 'away' but a noun: an out is a way of escape
not 'unwell' but 'a kind of': this is a type of escape, one a suspect offers the police

explanation.surface: Someone is feeling a bit unwell.
explanation.walkthrough: Out of sorts means unwell, but read it as 'an out of sorts': an alibi is a kind of way out.
explanation.definitionFit: A reading by category: an alibi is a claim of being elsewhere that gets a suspect off, a sort of out.

explanation.surface: A parent loses control of a toddler.
explanation.walkthrough: Lose control of reads as losing a grip on the child, but only Lose control is the definition, as a car does on ice.
explanation.definitionFit: A driving sense: a vehicle sliding on a slippery road, out of the driver's control.

definitions.meaning: to freeze is to stop moving entirely
a checkout worker looks after the cash register; the question mark flags the pun

explanation.surface: A shop worker at the checkout stands frozen to the spot.
explanation.walkthrough: The second reading splits the answer as KEEPS TILL; a till is a cash register.
explanation.definitionFit: A command to stop moving, and a pun: the checkout worker minds the till.

indicators.note: the answer is held within the words that follow

parts.note: the last three letters of joint and the first two of won't, across the comma

explanation.surface: Something fixed with a proper joint will not come apart.
explanation.walkthrough: The comma between joint and won't is ignored; the answer runs across it.
explanation.definitionFit: An adverbial phrase: something split has been divided into two parts.

clue.text: Row onto sandy hill where NZ craft may berth

indicators.note: the row is added onto the end of the hill

parts.note: a dune is a sandy hill
a row (rhymes with cow) is a noisy din

explanation.surface: Rowing a boat up onto a sand dune, looking for a harbour in New Zealand.
explanation.walkthrough: Row suggests rowing a boat, which suits the harbour, but it is the noise, a din. Dunedin is a port city in New Zealand's South Island.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by description: a harbour city on New Zealand's South Island where boats berth.

clue.text: Turn pine over to show wood

indicators.note: the word for pine is turned over

parts.note: to pine for something is to have a YEN for it; turned over

explanation.surface: A carpenter turns a piece of pine over to show off the grain.
explanation.walkthrough: Pine and wood suggest timber, but pine is the verb meaning to long for. A spinney is a British word for a small wood.
explanation.definitionFit: A British word for a small wood or copse, the wood of the clue being trees, not timber.
